name: Hilaria

project_scope.caution: Hilaria mutica also appears as Pleuraphis mutica in regional taxonomies. This is the SAME concept, not a second admission.

look_here_first: START AT GROUND LEVEL, NOT THE SEEDHEAD. CURLYMESQUITE Hilaria belangeri: usually SHORT creeping turf, long slender ABOVEGROUND ROOTING STOLONS with hairy nodes, often tightly curling narrow dead leaves. TOBOSA Hilaria mutica (Pleuraphis mutica in other treatments): taller stiff coarse grass with short THICK SCALY RHIZOMES BELOWGROUND, no long surface stolons. Each can carry one compact, terminal, spike-like head with THREE-SPIKELET groups; a post-fruiting zigzag central axis is not enough to name either. New photo lesson below now features true existing source-identified head photos and grass habit views, with eight arrows on broad visible structures only. Definitive continuous stolon and belowground attached rhizome are BOTH still unphotographed. This is a field-ready comparison with actual morphological photo gaps, not a fully confirmed diagnostic photo key.

recognition.where_to_look_first: Inspect continuous stems at soil surface first, then the sheath/ligule and leaf size, THEN the compact terminal spikelet fascicles. Both species have grouped 3-spikelet flowering units, so zigzag fruiting rachis by itself cannot distinguish them.

comparison_lesson.memory_rule: LOW RUNNERS ABOVE GROUND = CURLYMESQUITE. TOUGH SCALY RHIZOMES BELOW GROUND = TOBOSA.
quick_split: H. belangeri — usually 10–30 cm tall with fine wiry stolons spreading across surface; hairy rooting nodes; green-to-golden finely curled leaves; short solitary seedhead.
H. mutica — usually 30–70 cm taller coarse stems, buried thick scaly rhizomes, no stolons; stiffer often ashy leaves and more substantial short spike of three-spikelet clusters.
comparison_lesson.taxonomic_note: Tobosa = Hilaria mutica = Pleuraphis mutica in some treatments. Do not install or count two separate species cards for those names.
comparison_lesson.lookalike_warning: Cynodon dactylon, Bouteloua dactyloides and Hopia obtusa can all grow in turf/runners, but have different true reproductive architecture; compare attached rootstock and seedheads before deciding.

what_to_teach_crew: If the plant is dormant, don't assume all pale sod is bermudagrass: look for small CURLED blades and wiry hairy stolons of curlymesquite.
Stolons are aboveground runners; rhizomes are underground stems. This distinction often beats flowering color.
A true grass ligule belongs at the joint between sheath and blade—show it with a millimeter ruler, not an unseen arrow.
Group-of-THREE spikelets and residual zigzag rachis indicate the Hilaria-type fruiting head, but they do not split these two species.
Avoid digging in sensitive restoration sites; only expose/photograph rhizomes where authorized, then restore soil.
Pleuraphis mutica is the older/alternate tobosa combination, not a third canonical species.

In ambiguous Hilaria specimens: FIRST trace a real live attached stem. ABOVEground wiry rooted runner implies curlymesquite; BELOWground short scaly rhizome implies tobosa. Our gallery is a good head/habit key, but does not yet photograph either attached rootstock.
visual_needs: Hilaria belangeri: ONE linked ABOVEGROUND stolon connecting two rooted tufts, with visible hairy node at scale — TOP PRIORITY
Hilaria mutica: actual thick SCALY UNDERGROUND rhizome attached to a shoot — TOP PRIORITY; do not mistake soil roots or leaf sheaths
Both Hilaria: truly DISSECTED 3-spikelet fascicle next to empty zigzag axis, measured in mm
Both Hilaria: genuine membranous ligule of same-stage material with a mm scale
Both species: final owner mobile position QA and independent exact-species determination of provisional source photo images

comparison_cards.title: Curlymesquite versus tobosa — ground-level growth
comparison_cards.look_here_first: Uninterrupted ABOVEGROUND wiry stolon with rooting hairy nodes = CURLYMESQUITE. Thick SCALY BELOWGROUND rhizome with a stiff upright sod base but no long aboveground runners = TOBOSA.

field_matrix.tobosa: Stiff ~30–70 cm culms, range overlaps with grazed plants

field_matrix.curlymesquite: LONG surface stolon roots at leafy nodes (hairy)
field_matrix.tobosa: Short buried THICK SCALY rhizome, stolons absent

field_matrix.curlymesquite: Thin narrow, often curls after drying
field_matrix.tobosa: Stiffer usually broader, ashen and dry in drought

field_matrix.curlymesquite: Short terminal spike of clusters of 3
field_matrix.tobosa: More substantial spike with groups of 3, not exclusive

comparison_cards.photo_evidence: Archived species-labeled field photos show leaves and short vs taller spikes, not connected stems under/above the soil. These are real PHOTO GAPS.
comparison_cards.warning: Do not call the species on grass height, yellow/brown color or one short flowering head.

comparison_cards.title: The 3-spikelet Hilaria fascicle — shared identity, NOT species splitter
comparison_cards.look_here_first: Both Hilaria concepts have compact one-axis heads bearing clusters/fascicles of THREE spikelets. Fascicles fall off as a unit to expose zigzag-like flowering axis. A source photo of a clustered head demonstrates gross shape, not a counted dissection.
comparison_cards.photo_evidence: New photo panels show repeated visibly grouped structures along spikes; individual central/lateral member anatomical counts cannot be verified from this scale.
comparison_cards.warning: Need 5-mm macro comparing one attached intact group and empty rachis from a verified specimen.

comparison_cards.title: Curlymesquite versus bermudagrass, buffalograss and vine mesquite
comparison_cards.look_here_first: All can occur as LOW TURF. Bermuda has radiating 3–7 seedhead fingers and both stolons/rhizomes; buffalograss has separate male and female reproductive shoots; vine mesquite has longer rooting stolons and different panicle architecture. Curlymesquite's compact solitary spike and hairy rooting nodes support the ID together.
comparison_cards.photo_evidence: Species source photos show curled low leaves and compact heads; no complete runners with actual hairy rooted nodes yet.
comparison_cards.warning: Do not call any dormant grass sod 'native curlymesquite' without confirming its node/seedhead.

comparison_cards.title: Tobosa versus vine mesquite and clumped short grasses
comparison_cards.look_here_first: A stiff TOBOSA clump has scaly underground rhizomes while vine mesquite and curlymesquite use surface rooting stolons. Even dry-season gray broad foliage is not proof. Trace true connected stem underground before labeling.
comparison_cards.photo_evidence: New photo shows coarse clumps and condensed spike, not belowground rhizome tissue.
comparison_cards.warning: The name Pleuraphis mutica belongs to the same grass as Hilaria mutica in our working project, not an extra canonical learner card.
